analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and federal employees from trading stocks on inside government information.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it sat in committee until 2012, when its sponsor filed a petition to force a vote with 286 cosponsors backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for members of Congress, congressional staff, and other federal employees to buy or sell stocks or commodities while holding nonpublic information about upcoming legislation or government decisions. It would also require faster disclosure of members' stock trades and force 'political intelligence' firms that gather inside tips for investors to register and disclose their clients. The bill never received a House vote; its sponsor filed a discharge petition to force it out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors, who today can be on the losing end of trades made with insider knowledge of pending legislation; the integrity of markets generally; and members of Congress who want to avoid the appearance of profiting from their positions.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the SEC and CFTC to write rules banning trading on nonpublic information about pending legislation obtained from members or employees of Congress, closing an enforcement gap that otherwise leaves congressional insider trading largely unpoliced.
Requires members and legislative-branch employees to report stock, bond, and commodities futures transactions of $1,000 or more within 90 days, instead of only on annual forms.

Brings political intelligence consultants — firms that gather information from government officials on behalf of investment clients — under the lobbying disclosure law's registration and reporting requirements, and subjects them to annual audits by the Comptroller General.

Adds a rule to the House Code of Official Conduct barring House members, officers, and employees from disclosing nonpublic legislative information when they have reason to believe it will be used for trading.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and federal employees who trade securities would face new disclosure and trading restrictions. Political intelligence firms would bear new registration and reporting costs. Wall Street firms and hedge funds that buy information from congressional sources would lose access to a source of trading advantage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress, staff, and political intelligence firms

drawbacks.text: The trading ban leaves room for judgment calls: 'material nonpublic information' about legislation must be defined by regulators, and legitimate policy research could be swept in or genuine insider trades escape a narrow definition.

The 90-day transaction reporting window is slower than the 30-45 day standards that critics of congressional trading have advocated, so the public would still learn of members' trades weeks after they occur.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem — trading on government information that ordinary investors cannot access — with enforcement mechanisms that already exist for corporate insiders. The main costs fall on the officials being regulated and on firms selling political intelligence, not on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House never took up the bill; after a year in committee, its sponsor filed a discharge petition to force a vote, which did not reach the required signatures before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 17, 2011 and referred to six committees, an unusually broad referral that fragmented it among committees with different jurisdictions.
On March 29, 2011, the committees were discharged and the bill was re-referred, again to multiple committees; no committee reported it to the floor in 2011.
The House held committee hearings on the bill in December 2011, but it still never reached the floor for a vote.
On February 1, 2012, sponsor Rep. Walz filed a discharge petition (Petition 112-3) to force the bill out of committee and onto the floor.
The bill's 286 cosponsors — 187 Democrats and 99 Republicans — far outnumbered the 218 signatures a discharge petition requires, yet the bill never received a floor vote in the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their staff kept the ability to trade on nonpublic legislative information without the new disclosure requirements this bill would have imposed. Political intelligence firms kept operating outside the lobbying disclosure regime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress, staff, and political intelligence firms

for.name: Rep. Tim Walz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and filed a discharge petition to force a floor vote after it stalled in committee.

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor.

for.name: 286 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority support from both parties in the House.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and committee chairs controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House vote during the 112th Congress, despite its bipartisan majority of cosponsors and a discharge petition filed to force action.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill but never reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily bipartisan (187 Democrats and 99 Republicans), so the bill's lack of a floor vote cannot be explained by party-line opposition on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would force firms that sell legislators' and regulators' information to investors to register and disclose their activities. Today they operate outside lobbying disclosure rules, keeping their client lists and contacts confidential.

industries.industry: Wall Street trading firms and hedge funds
industries.note: The bill would restrict trading on legislative information obtained from congressional sources and require disclosure of members' transactions, reducing an informational edge available to well-connected investors but not to the general public.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior staff
industries.note: The bill's trading and disclosure restrictions apply directly to these officeholders. The restriction serves the public interest in fair markets; the cost falls on those being regulated.
The bill extends the same insider-trading ban to commodities and swaps, so traders using nonpublic legislative information in those markets would face new CFTC rules.
